headline: July US CPI print this morning is the day's single biggest market swing factor
tldr: July US CPI due at 13:30 BST; June surprised soft at 3.5%, but Hormuz tensions have worsened since.
US stocks fell Tuesday as Iran vowed to keep Hormuz shut; crude near $83, 10-year Treasury at 4.73%.
UK motor insurance projected to worsen to 108% NCR in 2026 as rate cuts feed through to earned premium.
Milton Keynes officially submitted its UK City of Culture 2029 bid, with shortlist expected this autumn.
PM Burnham faces pressure over early release of PC Harper's killers as probation officers vote for strike action.

sections.title: Markets
sections.body:
**Markets — Wednesday 12 August 2026**

The big development overnight: 
the July CPI print is due from the BLS at 8:30 a.m. ET this morning
 — so markets Tuesday were effectively on hold, waiting for it. The June CPI (the most recent confirmed read) 
came in at 3.5%, the first decline in five months, beating expectations of 3.8%
, driven by an easing in energy costs as 
energy inflation fell to 15.7% from 23.5% in May
. 
Core inflation also eased to 2.6% from 2.9%, undershooting the 2.8% forecast
. That's the constructive backdrop — but it's June data, and Hormuz has since deteriorated again.

Tuesday's session reflected the impasse. 
US stocks slipped as the US-Iran standoff intensified: the Dow fell ~0.3%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.3%, and the Nasdaq fell ~0.6%
. The proximate cause: 
US crude settled near $83 as Iran reiterated plans to keep the waterway shut until its demands are met
, while 
President Trump rebuked Iran's demand for reparations, saying he would wait for economic pressure to build
 — hardening the stalemate. 
Treasury yields moved higher as energy tensions weighed on rate expectations, with the 10-year rising 3 basis points to 4.73%
.


Asian stocks were poised to follow Wall Street lower, with traders holding back from riskier bets ahead of CPI and remaining wary over US-Iran developments
. 
Tokyo reopened after a public holiday on Tuesday
 — IJPN's +0.27% in Sam's ISA suggests a modest catch-up bounce.

European equities are in a different register. 
The Stoxx 600 hit its fourth consecutive record close last Friday, with the DAX, CAC 40, FTSE 100, and FTSE MIB all posting gains
, driven partly by solid earnings flow and partly by the euro's resilience buffering energy cost pass-through.

**In Sam's portfolio:** ASML's +3.80% is the standout — a meaningful divergence from recent tech softness, likely driven by order flow or analyst commentary specific to the stock rather than broad sector sentiment. AMD +1.01% is a modest recovery from Monday's Nvidia-led drag. The defence names are mixed: QinetiQ +1.42% continues its run; BAE -0.62% and Rolls-Royce -0.45% are giving back some of last week's geopolitical premium, possibly on thin summer volumes rather than any fundamental shift.

**Watch:** Today's July CPI at 13:30 BST is the swing factor. The June print surprised soft — if July repeats that, rate-cut expectations will revive and tech/growth names should bounce. A hot print, with oil back above $84, would validate the 4% Fed funds pricing and cap equities.

sections.body:
**Deadline: Friday 21 Aug, 17:30 BST — 9 days away**

**Prices**


Prices remain locked until the GW1 deadline; the market only opens after that.
 Nothing to chase on this front — squad finalisation is still the job.

**Injuries — what's new**

The big Sunderland update: 
Regis Le Bris has said both Mukiele and Alderete "should be on the bench against Ipswich" in GW1.
 That's a meaningful downgrade from the bare 75% flag — bench appearances only means minimal attacking returns, and the knock flags remain live. Avoid both for GW1; the fixture appeal evaporates if they're not starting.


Saliba remains the biggest defensive absence
 heading into the opener — a notable consideration if you're building Arsenal's backline.

**Differentials — any movement?**

No major shifts in the community consensus since yesterday. 
Anderson and Amad continue to feature as value differential picks at the £6.0m–£6.5m bracket.
 
Gabriel is flagged as a genuine differential captain option for the brave, given his set-piece threat and clean-sheet upside.



Doku and Foden sit in a middle ground — City's fixture run makes them attractive for a 3–4 gameweek hold, but their lower xGI/90 makes them rotation-dependent rather than banker differentials.


**Main action today: confirm your starting XI is free of bench-risk doubts before Friday.**

sections.title: Data & BI
sections.body:
**Data & BI**

The most substantive new item this week is a **dbt Core release**. 
dbt Core 1.12.0 dropped as a major update, bringing breaking changes, expanded semantic layer and v2 YAML support, a bundled dbt-state plugin, a new v2 parser option, and `dbt login`.
 The semantic layer angle is the most relevant part for most teams: 
it adds `UnparsedMetricV2` support to read in new-style YAML Semantic Layer Metrics
, alongside v2 parser improvements. If you're running dbt Core in production, check the breaking changes list before upgrading.

On the **Power BI** side, the July feature summary (published last week) is worth a skim beyond the settings pane rollout already covered. 
The July 2026 update introduces new capabilities across reporting, modelling, mobile, and embedded analytics — highlights include expanded modern visual defaults, conditional formatting improvements for line charts and legends, Model Options in the Power BI Service, and TMDL View on the web.
 The TMDL-in-browser item is worth noting: 
developers can now script, modify, and apply changes to model objects directly in a code editor using Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL)
 without leaving the service.

**BigQuery** covered yesterday; nothing materially new beyond those posts.

- 
PBIR is scheduled to be enabled by default in Power BI Desktop in July/August, with GA to follow — worth confirming whether that's landed in your Desktop build.

sections.title: Career & Data Leadership
sections.body:
**Career & Data Leadership**

**The hiring market: deliberate, not dead**


Companies are still hiring, but with sharper criteria, longer pipelines, and greater scrutiny.
 
78% of UK hiring is now driven by replacement roles — resignations, departures, restructures — while just 20% is linked to genuine expansion.
 For senior data candidates, that means most live roles are backfills, not net-new headcount — worth knowing when you're reading between the lines of a JD.


Demand for data roles (architects, engineers, scientists) remains strong and growing, while the market for generalist tech skills will most likely stay flat.
 
Candidate mobility is also rising — 66% of data specialists are open to new opportunities this year.


**What data leaders are actually being asked to do in 2026**


Four areas now separate leaders from laggards: data quality management, modern data governance, functional AI governance, and data literacy investment — with best-in-class companies executing these fundamentals tactically, not just strategically.


A direct signal from Hex's State of Data Teams survey: 
AI tooling focus surged 24% among data teams in the second half of last year, knocking out "enabling self-serve" as the second biggest area of focus.
 If your team is still leading with self-serve as the pitch to executives, that framing is now dated.

**The leadership gap that's becoming structural**


Despite massive investments, many organisations still struggle to turn data into trusted business outcomes — and the gap between data volume and data value has never been wider.
 
The leaders cutting through this are connecting every data initiative to quantifiable business outcomes: better measurement frameworks, clearer ROI calculations, and ruthless prioritisation of high-impact projects.
 That's the conversation to drive upward.

sections.title: UK Insurance
sections.body:
**Motor losses: EY updates the picture**


EY's latest analysis forecasts the UK motor market will remain loss-making across both 2026 and 2027. After a 98% NCR in 2024, the market slipped back into the red in 2025 at an estimated 102% — and EY now projects a worse 108% for this year.
 
The weaker outlook is driven primarily by premium rate reductions since late 2024 now feeding through to earned premium, alongside continued claims inflation.
 
After premiums fell by nearly 12% during 2025, EY expects motor premiums to rise 4% in 2026 and a further 12% in 2027 as insurers respond to the cost pressure.


**FCA: rule simplification now live**


FCA insurance rule changes came into force in June and July 2026, with the key tranche effective 26 June and remaining provisions following on 27 July, as set out in Handbook Notice No. 142.
 
Building on its December 2025 Policy Statement, the FCA will continue streamlining its Handbook, leaning more heavily on Consumer Duty rather than introducing new product-specific requirements.
 
Further consultations are in train, including simplifying GAP insurance rules, general insurance pricing data requirements, and information disclosure obligations.
 The practical risk: firms updating disclosure and claims workflows mid-cycle face transitional compliance exposure even as the intent is deregulatory.

**Pure protection market study: conclusion imminent**


The FCA intends to conclude its pure protection market study later in 2026, with an emphasis on closing the "protection gap" and improving awareness and claims experiences.
 Less directly relevant to personal lines property/motor, but worth flagging for any teams with life or critical illness exposure.

**Tokio Marine backs UK carbon credit MGA**


Tokio Marine Group made an undisclosed strategic investment in Kita, a Lloyd's coverholder specialising in carbon credit insurance, expanding an existing Tokio Marine Kiln relationship into a broader partnership developing non-delivery insurance for Japanese carbon credit buyers.
 Niche, but signals continued appetite from major carriers to back specialist UK MGAs via balance-sheet rather than purely capacity arrangements.

sections.title: Milton Keynes
sections.body:
**Events — diary these**

- **📅 25 Aug** — [NatWest Tech Tuesdays](https://protospace.uk/events) networking, NatWest Community Hub, 11:30–13:00. *(Already flagged — confirming it's still on.)*

**Local news**

**City of Culture bid submitted.** 
MK officially launched its UK City of Culture 2029 bid yesterday, 10 August
, framing it around the city's "hippies in helicopters" founding myth. 
The final application deadline was today; shortlisted cities are expected to be announced this autumn.
 
The winner receives £10 million, with runners-up getting £125,000.
 Winning would coincide with a notable infrastructure milestone: 
MK's City of Culture year would align with the opening of a new £76 million, 4,000-capacity city-centre venue.
 For the tech community, worth noting that 
the bid is being led by MKCC in partnership with, among others, The Open University and Universal.


**Skills investment.** 
MK College is set to receive £410,000 from Milton Keynes City Council to deliver specialist adult training in health and social care, construction, logistics and the creative industries.
 Modest sum but signals the Lib Dem–Labour council directing resource at workforce pipeline.

**Labour market note.** 
Payrolled employment in MK fell 0.2% over the year to June 2026 — 308 fewer workers — with the monthly figure broadly unchanged.
 A small dip, not a trend yet, but worth watching given the wider data hiring market.

sections.title: News
sections.body:
Here is today's News section, based on what the searches surfaced for 12 August 2026:

---

**UK — PC Harper killers & early-release row.** 
Pressure is mounting on PM Andy Burnham over the early release of PC Harper's killers, with Burnham saying he is "confident" it can be halted.
 
The Telegraph reports Burnham is being accused of "throwing the Justice Secretary under the bus" over the affair.
 Probation officers have added fuel to the fire: 
they voted for strike action after warning that early releases are adding to excessive workloads.


**UK — Summer 2026 on course to be hottest ever.** 
The Met Office says summer 2026 is on course to be the UK's hottest on record, with the heatwave tipped to outstrip the record-breaking summer of 1976.
 Worth noting for energy demand and infrastructure stress.

**UK — GDP figures due.** 
The OBR's spring forecast put full-year UK growth at 1.1%, weaker than the 1.4% pencilled in at the Autumn Budget, with unemployment slightly higher than previously expected.
 Official Q2 figures land this week and will test whether that trajectory holds.

**UK — Bank taxes back in play.** 
The Burnham government has declined to rule out higher bank taxes ahead of the Budget, fuelling fresh speculation in what Bloomberg calls "silly season" fiscal briefings.


**Colombia earthquake — death toll rising.** 
The earthquake has killed at least 181 people and left 2,595 injured, with at least 195 officially missing — though civilian databases put that figure closer to 4,000.
 Search operations continue in Cali.

**Clacton by-election.** 
Nigel Farage faces a parliamentary by-election in Clacton-on-Sea this week, with his campaign finances under investigation.
 A strong Reform hold would reinforce the party's momentum; a scare would matter.
